whyCorrect: Track the chain of consequences the text sets up. Calling the novel autobiographical may lead readers to think Bronte only fictionalized things that really happened; and in a field that prizes creativity and inventiveness, thinking that means undervaluing the invention the book actually contains. The blank has to name that cost, so it must say the label makes Agnes Grey look like a smaller imaginative achievement than it is.

whyWrong.B: The passage says the parallels to Bronte's life are easy to see, not that other characters' real-world counterparts are hard to identify; nothing in the text sets up a difficulty of identification.
whyWrong.C: The text never says Bronte herself claimed the novel was based on real events, and it makes no recommendation about what she should have done — it describes how readers and critics label the work.
whyWrong.D: Disagreement among critics is never mentioned. The text describes one shared misperception, not a split in opinion.

commonMistakes: Choosing a statement that is merely related to the topic instead of the specific drawback the sentence is building toward.
tips: When a text ends in 'which can suggest that ______,' the blank is the last link in a stated chain — reread the sentence forward and ask what follows from the clause just before it.

whyCorrect: The result that needs explaining is that a keyword search for 'Twitter' returned a few papers about things like tractor-engine sounds. A database search matches the word, not the meaning, so the explanation has to be that the word itself has a second sense. 'Twitter' also names a chirping or rattling noise, so papers about machine noises legitimately contain the search term while having nothing to do with the website.

whyWrong.A: A conversation held on the platform about tractor engines would still make those papers about the social media site, and it does not explain why unrelated engine-noise research was indexed under the term.
whyWrong.B: This is probably true of the databases as a whole, but it says nothing about why the specific search for 'Twitter' pulled in engine-noise papers.
whyWrong.D: Announcing publications on Twitter would not put the word 'Twitter' into the text of a paper about tractor engines, so it explains nothing about the odd results.

tips: For 'one reasonable explanation is that ______,' pick the choice that accounts for the exact anomaly described, not one that is simply true.

whyCorrect: Look at what sits on each side of the blank. Before it you already have a complete sentence: Joy Williams's essay is just one of many essays included in Home Ground: A Guide to the American Landscape. After the blank you have another complete sentence: the book celebrates the rich language used to describe the landscape of North America. Two independent clauses need a full stop, so ending the first sentence and opening the second with the modifier 'Edited by Barry Lopez and Debra Gwartney,' is the only version that works.

whyWrong.A: 'Landscape, edited by Barry Lopez and Debra Gwartney,' still leaves 'the book celebrates...' joined to the first complete sentence by nothing but a comma — a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: Removing the comma does not fix the splice; two independent clauses are still run together with only a comma before 'the book.'
whyWrong.D: 'and edited by...' just extends the first clause, so 'the book celebrates...' is still spliced onto it with a comma.

commonMistakes: Choosing the punctuation that sounds smoothest around the participial phrase without checking what comes after the comma later in the sentence.

whyCorrect: The opening modifier 'Having climbed the charts for twenty-six weeks' has to describe whatever the blank refers to, and the only thing in the passage that climbed the charts is the song 'Pon de Replay' — one song, so the pronoun must be singular. 'It' is the only singular option.

whyWrong.A: 'They' is plural, and the passage names a single song, not multiple songs or performers.
whyWrong.C: 'Each' implies a group of items being taken one at a time, but only one song is under discussion.
whyWrong.D: 'Those' is plural and also vague — there is no plural noun for it to point back to.

tips: With an opening participial phrase, find the noun that actually performed the action before choosing the pronoun.

whyCorrect: Both halves of this sentence are complete: 'In many languages, including English, these consonants are rare' and 'in some dialects of Mandarin, however, four such consonants are relatively common.' Note that 'however' here is an interrupter inside the second clause, not a joining word, so it cannot hold the two clauses together. A semicolon is what separates two independent clauses without a conjunction.

whyWrong.A: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice; 'however' set off by commas does not license it.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation at all the two complete clauses run together into a fused sentence.
whyWrong.D: Comma plus 'and' would be legal punctuation, but 'and' signals addition while the sentence draws a contrast that 'however' already marks, so the two joining words work against each other.

commonMistakes: Treating 'however' as if it were a conjunction like 'but' — it is an adverb, so it cannot join two sentences with only a comma.

whyCorrect: Strip out the phrase between the commas, 'of the Universidade Federal Fluminense in Brazil,' and the sentence is 'Anthropologist Livia Barbosa ______ food and sociability.' The subject is one person, so the verb must be singular present: 'studies.'

whyWrong.A: 'Have studied' is plural; a singular subject would need 'has studied.'
whyWrong.C: 'Study' is the plural present form and does not agree with the single anthropologist named.
whyWrong.D: 'Are studying' is plural; the singular would be 'is studying.'

tips: Cross out any phrase set off by commas before checking subject-verb agreement — it is placed there to hide the real subject.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence ending in 'the ultimate goal,' and everything after it, 'catching an in-person glimpse of all 10,000-plus species of birds,' is not a sentence — it is a phrase that names what that goal is. A colon after a complete clause is exactly the mark used to introduce an explanation or specification.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, 'the ultimate goal catching an in-person glimpse' runs the noun straight into the phrase and produces nonsense.
whyWrong.B: A period makes 'Catching an in-person glimpse of all 10,000-plus species of birds' a standalone fragment with no verb of its own.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and the material after the blank is only a phrase.

tips: Colon versus semicolon comes down to one test: what follows the mark. A semicolon needs a full sentence after it; a colon does not.

whyCorrect: The subject is Tarawa, a single place; 'with a population of roughly 30,000 people' is just an interrupting phrase. A singular subject in the present takes 'is,' giving 'Tarawa is home to an impressive 29 percent of Kiribati's total population.'

whyWrong.A: 'Are' is plural and cannot follow the singular subject Tarawa.
whyWrong.B: 'Are being' is both plural and an odd progressive for a permanent fact.
whyWrong.D: 'Have been' is plural; the singular present perfect would be 'has been,' and the sentence calls for simple present anyway.

commonMistakes: Letting the plural noun 'people' inside the interrupting phrase pull the verb into the plural.

whyCorrect: The clause before the blank states a cause: the plant pulls a large amount of chromium out of the ground and locks it away in its roots and shoots. The clause after states the effect of that: the chromium level in the soil goes down. 'In turn' is the transition that marks one thing following as a consequence of the other.

whyWrong.A: 'In addition' would present the falling soil concentration as a separate extra fact, but it is the direct result of the absorption just described.
whyWrong.B: 'Nevertheless' signals a contrast, and there is no contrast — the second clause is exactly what you would expect after the first.
whyWrong.D: 'Specifically' introduces a narrower restatement of the same idea, but the drop in soil chromium is a new, downstream outcome, not a detail of the absorption itself.

tips: Ask whether the second clause is a result, an addition, a contrast, or a restatement before scanning the choices.

whyCorrect: Bryan opposed a strong central government and opposed ratifying the Constitution. What follows is that his published essays attacked the federalists, who wanted the Constitution adopted. That is precisely what someone with his stated views would be expected to write, so the transition needs to mark consistency between belief and action.

whyWrong.A: 'By comparison' sets up a comparison between two different things, but both halves describe the same man's single position.
whyWrong.C: 'Nevertheless' announces a contrast, yet attacking federalists is in perfect agreement with being an anti-federalist.
whyWrong.D: 'In other words' would mean the second clause restates the first, but it adds new information about what he published and where.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a claim: the pseudonym accomplished far more than hiding his name. The second sentence then presses that same claim harder, spelling out that it was a complex rhetorical strategy that borrowed the authority of Roman republicanism. When a sentence intensifies and confirms the claim just made, 'Indeed' is the transition.

whyWrong.B: 'Conversely' requires the second sentence to state the opposite, but it agrees with and strengthens the first.
whyWrong.C: 'In addition' would frame the second sentence as a separate new point; it is instead the same point developed.
whyWrong.D: 'However' signals a reversal that never occurs — nothing in the second sentence qualifies or undercuts the first.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize a similarity, so the sentence has to name something both works share. The notes list Mater as acrylic and oil stick on canvas and Flash in Naples as acrylic, oil stick, and oil on canvas — acrylic appears in both. Saying that both works use acrylic as a medium is the only choice built around a shared feature.

whyWrong.A: Calling Mater the larger of the two states a difference in size, the opposite of what the question asks for.
whyWrong.C: Giving one completion date and then the other presents a sequence of two different years rather than pointing out anything the works have in common.
whyWrong.D: The word 'while' frames the two lists of materials as a contrast, so this emphasizes how the works differ.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that accurately uses the notes but serves the wrong purpose — accuracy is not enough when the stem names a specific goal.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is to emphasize where the figures are positioned in Lost in the Shuffle. Only one choice reports a position: the two young men occupy the bottom left and upper right corners of the canvas. Everything else in the notes — size, color, mood — is irrelevant to that goal.

whyWrong.A: This compares canvas dimensions, which is size, not the placement of the figures.
whyWrong.B: This describes the colors Rawles uses for the water and never mentions where anyone is positioned.
whyWrong.D: This is about the mood the paintings evoke and about how many figures appear, not where they are.

tips: Underline the goal in the stem and reject any choice that does not deliver exactly that, however true it is.

whyCorrect: The goal is to give an example of a specimen's nickname, which means the sentence has to actually state a nickname. Only one choice names one: Pops, the Triceratops specimen at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.

whyWrong.A: This says nicknames are given and points to a museum, but it never supplies the nickname itself, so no example is provided.
whyWrong.B: This describes the specimen's genus, period, and location without ever mentioning a nickname.
whyWrong.C: This is a general statement that specimens exist worldwide and are often nicknamed — background, not an example.

whyCorrect: The end of the sentence gives you the definition you need: the speeches in the blank are described as having 'unyielding rhetoric.' So the blank must mean rigid and uncompromising, the opposite of the nuanced, compromise-friendly views named earlier. 'Dogmatic' means asserting positions as unquestionably true and refusing to budge.

whyWrong.B: 'Vacillating' means wavering back and forth, which is the reverse of unyielding.
whyWrong.C: 'Banal' means dull and unoriginal; a speech can be banal and still be full of compromise, so it does not create the contrast the sentence needs.
whyWrong.D: 'Disingenuous' means insincere, which is about honesty rather than rigidity, and nothing in the text raises the question of sincerity.

tips: When a later phrase in the sentence characterizes the blank ('the unyielding rhetoric of the latter'), treat it as a supplied definition.

whyCorrect: The sentence says certain features are almost always present in mosque design and gives the minaret as the example, then adds that even stylistically mixed mosques include these standard features. The blank therefore needs a word meaning a defining, characteristic feature. 'Hallmark' is exactly that.

whyWrong.B: 'Rejection' would mean the minaret is something mosque architecture refuses, contradicting the statement that it is almost always included.
whyWrong.C: 'Motivation' would make the tower a reason for building rather than a design feature, which does not fit 'certain features are almost always included.'
whyWrong.D: 'Duplication' means a copy, but the point is that the minaret is a typical element, not that it reproduces something else.

whyCorrect: The second sentence gives the word away: it says consumers 'react the opposite way' when prices fall. So the blank in the first sentence must describe consumers reacting to a price change — they respond to a price increase by buying less. 'Respond to' is the only choice that names a reaction.

whyWrong.A: 'Differ from' would mean consumers are unlike rising prices, which is not a sensible comparison and does not describe behavior.
whyWrong.B: 'Think of' describes an opinion, but the sentence describes what consumers actually do — purchase fewer products.
whyWrong.D: 'Agree with' treats a price increase as a proposal to accept or reject, and buying less is not agreement.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets up a gap: 97 km/hr for the swordfish against 320 km/hr for the golden eagle, with the swordfish 'significantly slower.' The blank names that gap, and the rest of the sentence explains why such a gap is expected, since water imposes limits air does not. 'Disparity' means a marked inequality between two things.

whyWrong.A: 'Competition' would imply the animals are racing each other, which the text never suggests.
whyWrong.B: 'Equivalence' means the speeds are equal, contradicting 'significantly slower.'
whyWrong.C: 'Interaction' implies the two speeds act on one another; they are simply being compared.

whyCorrect: The second sentence supplies the benchmark: neutron-star-merger bursts usually last under 2 seconds. GRB 230307A lasted 200 seconds, a hundred times longer than typical. The blank must label it as something that departs from the norm, and 'an oddity' does exactly that.

whyWrong.B: 'A coincidence' means two things happening together by chance; nothing here is co-occurring, the burst is simply far longer than expected.
whyWrong.C: 'A reprieve' means a temporary relief from something unpleasant, which has no meaning for a burst's duration.
whyWrong.D: 'An incident' just means an event, so it would not register the contrast with the 2-second norm that the next sentence sets up.

tips: When a following sentence gives a typical value, the blank almost always names how the case at hand relates to that norm.

whyCorrect: Take the text one sentence at a time. Sentence one defines community science and calls it effective. Sentence two lists what it offers: insight into scientific life, youth interest, and more data. Sentence three names Merrill's butterfly study as a case where it was used. Definition, then benefits, then an example — that is the sequence in the correct choice.

whyWrong.A: The text never traces how community science developed over time, and it proposes no future projects.
whyWrong.B: The topic introduced is the research approach, not a study, and no results of the butterfly study are given — only that community science was essential to it.
whyWrong.D: The text does not argue for a new approach or report any public opinion about it; it states benefits as established.

commonMistakes: Choosing a structure choice because its last third matches; every part of the description has to match.

whyCorrect: The author's point is that copying one feature of Vancouver will not reproduce its pedestrian traffic, because many factors shape walking decisions and 'none of these factors in isolation fully explains pedestrian habits.' The amenities are introduced as the example of such a single feature. So the author would treat them as one contributing factor among several, not as the explanation.

whyWrong.A: The text never claims amenities reduce walkability anywhere; it only denies that copying them alone will raise pedestrian traffic.
whyWrong.B: The author never reverses the causal direction — nothing suggests the amenities are a product of the foot traffic rather than a contributor to it.
whyWrong.C: The text lists demographics and commuting distance as factors studies have highlighted, but it ranks nothing; its whole point is that no single factor dominates.

tips: 'None of these factors in isolation' is the sentence the question turns on — it rules out both ranking and dismissal.

whyCorrect: Emerson calls scholars the priests of thought who 'stand for the spiritual interest of the world,' and says it would be a shared disaster if they abandoned that role in a country where material interest dominates. Put plainly: in a materialistic society, someone must keep intellectual and spiritual life alive. That is the claim the passage builds to.

whyWrong.A: Military experience is never mentioned; the passage is about scholars, whatever their profession.
whyWrong.B: Emerson says the country's material interest is predominant, not that intellectuals themselves are preoccupied with material things — his worry is that they might abandon their post, not that they already have.
whyWrong.C: The passage does not discuss how others describe scholars or complain that descriptions undervalue them; it asserts their importance directly.

whyCorrect: This is a locate-the-detail question, so find the sentence naming her method. The first sentence says Villasana works by 'applying colorful yarn to photographs of people.' Yarn is the material stated.

whyWrong.A: Stone is never mentioned; her surfaces are photographs, not carved material.
whyWrong.B: Chalk appears nowhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: The text mentions an artist and portraits, which makes paint feel plausible, but the material specified is yarn applied to photographs.

tips: For 'according to the text' questions, point to the exact words that answer it before checking the choices.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts: Winnemucca speaks directly to the reader, and she does so to explain a custom. The quotation has to do both. Only one addresses a reader ('my dear reader') and then explains a practice — why Paiute people call good people father or mother.

whyWrong.B: This does describe a custom, naming girls after flowers, but it is narration addressed to no one; the reader is never spoken to.
whyWrong.C: This is family narrative about a grandfather's absence and a baby's birth, with neither a direct address nor an explanation of a custom.
whyWrong.D: This does address 'dear readers,' but it declines to describe the scene rather than explaining any custom, so it satisfies only half the claim.

commonMistakes: Accepting a quotation that matches one half of a two-part claim.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is specific: the greenlets treat the antshrike's alarm call as a danger signal. The obvious hole is that the birds might freeze or scatter at any sudden loud sound, alarm call or not. A control in which random noise produced no reaction closes that hole, showing the response is tied to the alarm call itself rather than to noise in general.

whyWrong.B: Other species reacting to the call says something about those species; it does not rule out the possibility that H. ochraceiceps is simply startled by loud sound.
whyWrong.C: Consistency across different callers shows the response is not tied to one individual antshrike, but it still leaves open whether any loud sound would do the same.
whyWrong.D: Birds freezing when the researchers merely approached, before any playback, weakens the conclusion by suggesting the reaction can be triggered by something other than the call.

tips: For 'which finding would support' questions, first name the alternative explanation that would sink the conclusion, then pick the choice that eliminates it.

whyCorrect: The researchers' claim is not that shielding had no effect; it is that the first phase cannot tell them how much of the drop is due to honeybees specifically. That claim holds if the shielding kept out pollinators besides honeybees, because then the 40 to 90 percent loss reflects the absence of all of them together. Squash bees also pollinating cucumbers, and also being blocked, is exactly that.

whyWrong.A: Ruling out a sunlight confound makes the shielding experiment cleaner, which if anything cuts against the claim that its results are hard to attribute.
whyWrong.B: This is about Chinese cabbage, not cucumbers, so it says nothing about what the cucumber shielding excluded.
whyWrong.D: How often honeybees are used on one crop versus another does not address what the shielding blocked or how to apportion the yield loss.

commonMistakes: Reading the claim as 'honeybees do not matter' rather than 'this experiment cannot isolate honeybees.'

whyCorrect: The key sentence says that for every class of animals examined, some individual studies showed differences well above the average for fish. Birds are one of those classes, so some bird studies exceeded the fish average. Any average has values below it, so those bird studies also exceeded some fish studies. That is what the blank must conclude.

whyWrong.A: The text never reports whether studies described the effects as harmful or beneficial, so nothing supports a claim about which studies specified detriment.
whyWrong.B: This reverses the stated result: on average, fish studies showed larger differences than bird studies.
whyWrong.C: The text gives no information comparing the Wysocki study's magnitude to the average for carp studies; Wysocki is mentioned only as an example that noise affects animals.

tips: 'Above the average for fish' is a statement about individual studies, not about class averages — keep the two levels separate.

whyCorrect: The contrast the text draws is about how hoards were found, not what was in them. Since the 1960s, metal detectors, radar, and aerial surveys let searchers pinpoint a hoard before digging. Take that technology away, as for the 1921 Auchnacree find, and there is no way to know a hoard is there in advance, so discoveries would have to come by chance while the ground was disturbed for some other reason.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text connects the era of discovery to what the hoards contained, so gold jewelry is unsupported.
whyWrong.C: Same problem: the passage never links discovery method to the age or rarity of the items found.
whyWrong.D: This reverses the logic. It is the modern technologies that let searchers locate hoards before putting a shovel in the ground; earlier finds came after the ground was already being disturbed.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences: 'light intensity affects the chemical reaction rate of photosynthesis' and 'as light intensity increases, so does the rate at which the reactants are converted into their products.' The second explains the first, spelling out what that effect looks like. A colon after a complete clause is the mark for introducing that kind of elaboration.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two independent clauses fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.C: 'And' joining two independent clauses needs a comma before it, and the choice supplies none; it also flattens an explanation into a simple addition.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: There is already an opening dash before 'assuming,' which starts an interrupting phrase inside the sentence. Punctuation that opens with a dash has to close with a dash. Choosing 'cooperation—this' closes the aside and lets the main clause run on as 'Walston's findings indicate that this practice has the potential to increase...'

whyWrong.A: With no mark at all the opening dash is never closed, and 'cooperation this practice' runs together.
whyWrong.B: A colon cannot serve as the closing half of a dash pair, and it would wrongly signal that an explanation follows.
whyWrong.D: A comma cannot close an interruption that was opened with a dash; the marks must match.

tips: Whenever you see one dash already in the sentence, look for the answer that supplies its partner.

whyCorrect: 'Along with others such as Lorenzo Thomas and Gwendolyn Brooks' is set off by commas, and phrases beginning with 'along with' never change the number of the subject. The subject is the writer Maya Angelou, one person, so the verb is singular: 'is commonly associated.'

whyWrong.A: 'Have been' is plural; the singular would be 'has been.'
whyWrong.C: 'Are' is plural and agrees with the names inside the interrupting phrase rather than with the actual subject.
whyWrong.D: 'Were' is plural, and the past tense also clashes with the ongoing fact that Angelou is associated with the movement.

commonMistakes: Treating 'along with' like 'and' — only 'and' creates a compound plural subject.

whyCorrect: 'A lawyer and cycling advocate' is an appositive describing Ernesto Hernandez-Lopez, and it interrupts the sentence between the subject and its verb 'has identified.' A nonessential appositive needs a comma on both sides; leaving out either one leaves the sentence half-punctuated.

whyWrong.A: With no commas at all, the appositive is jammed into the subject and the reader cannot tell where the subject ends.
whyWrong.C: This closes the appositive without opening it, so the name and description run together.
whyWrong.D: This opens the appositive without closing it, leaving 'has identified' stranded from its subject.

tips: Interrupting descriptions take two commas or none, never one.

whyCorrect: 'Dendrochronologist Valerie Trouet' is a single noun phrase: a job title used as a modifier directly in front of a name, like 'biologist Jane Smith.' Nothing separates a title from the name it modifies, so no punctuation belongs in the blank. The commas the sentence already has correctly set off the whole interrupter 'claims dendrochronologist Valerie Trouet.'

whyWrong.A: A colon must follow a complete clause and introduce something; here it would cut a title away from the name it belongs to.
whyWrong.B: A comma would turn 'Valerie Trouet' into a nonessential appositive after a bare occupation noun, breaking the title-plus-name unit and leaving 'claims dendrochronologist' dangling.
whyWrong.C: A dash creates an abrupt break in the middle of a noun phrase and would need a partner mark elsewhere.

tips: When the word before a name is a title or occupation used as a label, the correct answer is almost always no punctuation.

whyCorrect: Before the blank is a complete sentence: the relationship between genomes and epigenomes reveals how identical-DNA cells develop different functions. After the blank is another complete sentence, the 'whereas' clause plus its main clause about what the epigenome consists of, and it explains exactly how that difference arises. A colon after a full clause is the mark for introducing that explanation.

whyWrong.B: 'Functions and,' leaves a coordinating conjunction stranded before a comma and joins nothing correctly.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the two independent stretches fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.D: A comma makes 'whereas the genome in each cell contains a complete DNA sequence' attach to the first clause, and then 'the epigenome consists of...' is spliced on with only a comma.

whyCorrect: The clause before the semicolon states a cause: Betelgeuse got 40 percent brighter. The clause after states what followed from it: its brightness ranking climbed from 10th to 7th. The transition has to mark that consequence, and 'in turn' is the one that does.

whyWrong.A: 'In sum' introduces a summary of everything said, but a jump from 10th to 7th is a new consequence, not a wrap-up.
whyWrong.C: 'Specifically' would make the second clause a more precise restatement of the first, but ranking and percentage brightening are different measures, and one caused the other.
whyWrong.D: 'For example' would make the ranking change an instance of the 40 percent increase; it is the effect of that increase, not an example of it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the archways reflect the Modernista taste for organic, natural forms. The second says the stained glass and other decorative features also draw on nature. The word 'also' already signals that this is a second instance of the same pattern, so the transition must mark similarity.

whyWrong.B: 'By contrast' requires the second sentence to differ from the first, but both describe nature-inspired design.
whyWrong.C: 'In other words' means the second sentence restates the first; instead it adds a different set of features.
whyWrong.D: 'Nevertheless' signals a concession or reversal, and nothing in the second sentence pushes against the first.

tips: When the sentence after the blank already contains 'also' or 'too,' the transition is almost always additive.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a broad statement about many elements being isolated soon after discovery. The blank sentence then pulls that generalization back, admitting it does not hold for every element, and the europium example follows. The transition has to signal that concession, and 'Granted' is the one that concedes a limit on what was just claimed.

whyWrong.A: 'For this reason' presents the second sentence as caused by the first, but quick isolation of bromine is not the reason other elements resisted isolation.
whyWrong.C: 'Likewise' claims the second sentence matches the first; it in fact states the exception to it.
whyWrong.D: 'In other words' would mean the sentences say the same thing, yet the second reverses the scope of the first from 'many' to 'not all.'

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize the sculpture's size, so the sentence has to give its actual dimensions. Only one choice reports them: roughly 2 feet wide and 9 feet tall. The others use the notes correctly but stop at the vague adjective 'large' or switch to a different attribute.

whyWrong.A: This describes Serra's work in general as 'large metal sculptures' but gives no dimensions and never identifies the sculpture in question.
whyWrong.B: This states the material, lead, which is a different fact entirely.
whyWrong.D: This is a general statement about Serra's materials and again offers no measurements.

commonMistakes: Accepting the word 'large' as emphasis on size when specific numbers are available in the notes.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is to emphasize the mass of Sirius A, so the sentence must both name Sirius A and give its mass. Only one choice does: 2.063 solar masses, which it also frames as heavier than the Sun, since one solar mass equals the Sun's mass. That framing makes the number meaningful rather than just quoted.

whyWrong.A: This defines the unit and mentions Proxima Centauri; Sirius A never appears.
whyWrong.B: This is pure background about what a solar mass is and says nothing about Sirius A.
whyWrong.C: This compares the Sun with Proxima Centauri, which is the wrong star.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize the order in which the supercontinents formed, so the sentence has to put the two of them in sequence relative to each other. Ur formed about 3.1 billion years ago and Pangaea about 300 million years ago, so Pangaea came much later, and only one choice states that relationship.

whyWrong.A: This gives Ur's date and its breakup but never mentions Pangaea, so no ordering is established.
whyWrong.B: This says both were supercontinents and defines the term, which is a similarity, not a sequence.
whyWrong.D: This is a general description of the supercontinent cycle and names neither Ur nor Pangaea.

tips: To emphasize order, the sentence must relate the two items to each other, not just report a date for one.

whyCorrect: The colon means the second half explains why the ethicists' argument clashes with everyday usage. Their argument only works if having a helpful character means never acting otherwise, so situations that produce unhelpful behavior would disprove character. Kamtekar's reply is that ordinary usage never demanded that much: we call someone helpful if they are helpful often, not without exception. 'Unfailingly' names the impossibly strict standard the ethicists are assuming.

whyWrong.A: 'Self-servingly' describes motive, not consistency, and the ethicists' argument turns on how reliably a trait shows up.
whyWrong.B: 'Sporadically' means only now and then, which is weaker than 'frequently' rather than stronger — it would concede the ethicists' point instead of answering it.
whyWrong.C: 'Banal' means dull and unoriginal, an evaluation of quality that has nothing to do with how often someone acts helpfully.

tips: When a colon introduces the clause containing the blank, the blank has to do the explaining the colon promises.
commonMistakes: Reading 'not ______ helpful' as simply the opposite of 'frequently' and stopping there; the colon requires the blank to name the overdemanding standard the ethicists assume.

whyCorrect: The 'not only ... but also' frame pairs the blank with 'illuminate,' so the blank must be a verb of coming to understand something. What the fossil helps researchers do with the steps in hominid evolution is make them out. 'Discern' means to perceive or distinguish something that is hard to see.

whyWrong.A: 'Yield' means to produce; a fossil might yield information, but paleoanthropologists do not yield steps in evolution.
whyWrong.B: 'Exploit' means to take advantage of, which makes no sense applied to evolutionary steps and does not pair with 'illuminate.'
whyWrong.D: 'Prioritize' means to rank in importance, but the text is about learning what happened, not ordering it by importance.

whyCorrect: The rest of the sentence defines the blank for you: discoverers 'are not required to do so' and the choice is 'entirely' theirs. So naming is allowed but optional. 'Permissible' means allowed, which is precisely the middle ground between forbidden and required.

whyWrong.B: 'Infeasible' means impossible to do, yet the text gives 1083 Salvia as an example of a name that was in fact assigned.
whyWrong.C: 'Selective' describes a person or process that chooses carefully; it does not describe the status of an action within a set of conventions.
whyWrong.D: 'Mandatory' means required, which directly contradicts 'they are not required to do so.'

whyCorrect: The sentence says the mosque holds about 44,000 people and is one of the largest in the world, so the point is that almost nothing else is that big. 'Few religious buildings can be said to ______ the astonishing size' therefore needs a verb meaning to equal it. 'Match' does that.

whyWrong.A: 'Symbolize' would mean other buildings stand for the mosque's size, which is not a comparison of scale at all.
whyWrong.B: 'Conceal' would say other buildings hide the mosque's size, which makes no sense as a claim about their own dimensions.
whyWrong.C: 'Minimize' would mean other buildings make the size seem smaller, and saying few can do that gets the logic backwards.

whyCorrect: The fellowship exists to honor exceptional artists, so the reason Black was chosen has to be something praiseworthy she did for the arts over her lifetime. 'Contributions to' is the only phrase that names a positive body of work.

whyWrong.B: 'Doubts about' the arts would not be grounds for an award honoring exceptional artists.
whyWrong.C: 'Imitations of' the arts would describe copying rather than achievement and would not earn a lifetime honor.
whyWrong.D: 'Misunderstandings of' the arts is a failing, the opposite of what a fellowship recognizes.

whyCorrect: Read what the narrator claims about herself versus Celestine. She asserts a mental connection with Dot, says she understands things 'that her mother could not accept,' and states that Celestine 'never saw' Dot's impatience with babyhood. Every detail, including the bouncing in the stroller, is offered as evidence for the narrator's own superior insight into the child.

whyWrong.B: The narrator predicts nothing about Dot's future personality, and she presents Dot as unlike Celestine rather than similar to her.
whyWrong.C: Neither woman is described amusing Dot; Celestine takes pleasure in her softness and the narrator observes her, but no activity is done to entertain her.
whyWrong.D: Physical appearance is never mentioned for either woman.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the researchers' idea: Grande Terre's species belong to lineages older than the island's 80-million-year separation from Gondwana. The word 'however' then introduces Sundue's numbers, 8.5 million years for the island's Grammitis ferns and about 10.0 million for the region's, which are far too recent for that idea to hold for these ferns. So the text states a claim and then supplies findings that conflict with it.

whyWrong.A: The study does not explain why the researchers hold their view; it undercuts the view.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text says those researchers changed their minds after seeing the results.
whyWrong.C: The text presents the conflicting findings but never explains the discrepancy away.

commonMistakes: Reading 'however' as a signal that someone recanted rather than that the author is introducing counterevidence.

whyCorrect: The reason is stated in the sentence right before the algorithm is introduced: how you define a neighborhood and its boundaries is subjective. The team used the clustering algorithm to find dense groupings of amenities that correspond to neighborhoods people already recognize, such as Harvard Square. In other words, it replaced a subjective judgment with a repeatable, data-driven one.

whyWrong.A: The text never discusses business closings or their causes.
whyWrong.B: Consumer awareness and advertising are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
whyWrong.C: Predicting the mix of businesses is what the overall model does; the clustering algorithm's job was defining the neighborhood boundaries the model works within, and success of individual businesses is never discussed.

tips: 'So' in the sentence marks the causal link — the clause before it is the reason the question is asking for.

whyCorrect: The question asks for the conclusion, which is stated in the last sentence: the researchers concluded that setting 'no cutlery' as the default, plus other small app changes, could cut plastic waste by as much as 3.26 million metric tons a year. That is a claim that minor design tweaks produce a large reduction in waste.

whyWrong.A: The text projects a reduction from a design change, not a rise in China's plastic waste.
whyWrong.B: Nothing says any app prevents customers from requesting cutlery, only that the option is preselected, and app popularity trends are not discussed.
whyWrong.C: The study is about the effect of a default setting, not about customers understanding how apps work.

tips: Findings and conclusions are different sentences here — the finding is what the default did, the conclusion is what it implies at scale.

whyCorrect: The claim is that these sounds are aimed at predators rather than at other caterpillars of the same species. The strongest support is evidence that predators actually receive and act on the sounds. Chickens and yellow warblers breaking off attacks when they hear the sounds shows the signal works on predators, which is what 'directed primarily at predators' requires.

whyWrong.A: Sounds being distinctive to each species points toward species-specific communication, which is the alternative the researchers are arguing against.
whyWrong.C: This would undercut the claim for whistling species, since a sound predatory birds cannot detect could not be aimed at them.
whyWrong.D: How consistent an individual's repertoire is says nothing about who the sound is meant for.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis is that measuring nanoparticle buildup in zebra mussels could stand in for measuring it in vertebrates like common carp. A stand-in only works if the two species register nanoparticle levels the same way. Finding that D. polymorpha and C. carpio take up TiO2-NPs at comparable rates in comparable environments is exactly the correspondence a proxy needs.

whyWrong.B: Tolerating higher concentrations without harm is about the mussel's resilience, not about whether its readings predict the carp's.
whyWrong.C: Detecting low concentrations in one species and high concentrations in another compares two different measurement tasks and establishes no relationship between the species' burdens.
whyWrong.D: Greater individual-to-individual variability in the mussels would make them a noisier, less reliable stand-in, which weakens the hypothesis.

commonMistakes: Supporting the general idea that mussels are convenient study animals instead of the specific idea that their readings can substitute for carp readings.

whyCorrect: The claim has two halves that must appear in the same quotation: displeasure with poetry and recognition of its merit. Only one line does both, pairing 'a perfect contempt for it' with the discovery that 'there is in it after all, a place for the genuine.' That single sentence holds the ambivalence together.

whyWrong.A: This asserts that all these phenomena are important, which is affirmation with no note of displeasure.
whyWrong.B: This is criticism of what 'half poets' produce; it registers dissatisfaction but never credits poetry with merit.
whyWrong.C: This complains about derivative, unintelligible poems, again only the negative half of the claim.

tips: When a claim names two attitudes, reject any quotation that shows only one.

whyCorrect: Follow the count of studies. The positive association shows up in many North American studies and in other non-North American studies too, such as Luo's in China, while very few studies replicate Porvari and Verta's null result. That pattern makes the Finnish study the outlier and the association the general rule, so the blank must say the two levels typically rise and fall together in fresh water.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text reports absolute levels of carbon or mercury anywhere, only whether the two are correlated.
whyWrong.B: This is the hypothesis the last sentence undermines, since the correlation turns up outside North America as well.
whyWrong.D: The text gives no reason to doubt Luo's measurements; it treats that study as one of several that agree with the North American pattern.

whyCorrect: Two facts drive the inference. No source written before 1155 mentions the Round Table, and Preiddeu Annwfn was composed around 900. So Preiddeu Annwfn cannot contain any Round Table material, and Malory, whose compilation does include the Round Table, must have gotten it from somewhere else.

whyWrong.B: The text supports the first half but contradicts the second: since nothing before 1155 mentions the Round Table, no such stories were available to Geoffrey in the 1130s.
whyWrong.C: The passage says nothing about historical accuracy, and the date of Erec and Enide has no bearing on it.
whyWrong.D: No comparison of overall content between these works is offered; the only point of comparison is the presence or absence of the Round Table.

commonMistakes: Extending the one narrow fact about the Round Table into a broad claim about the works' general content or reliability.

whyCorrect: Look at the material after the blank. 'The hole's small size restricts light to a single ray' and 'all light passing through the hole can only arrive at a single destination' are two complete clauses joined by a comma, so one of them has to be made subordinate. Putting 'Because' at the front of the first turns it into a dependent clause, and the sentence before it ends cleanly at 'A ray diagram reveals how this works.'

whyWrong.A: 'Works because the hole's small size restricts light to a single ray' uses up the 'because,' leaving the following clause spliced on with a comma.
whyWrong.C: 'Works, it's because' splices two clauses together with a comma, and the later comma splice is still unfixed.
whyWrong.D: The colon is legal, but 'it's because the hole's small size restricts light to a single ray, all light... can only arrive' still runs two independent clauses together with only a comma.

tips: Check punctuation later in the sentence too — the blank often has to fix a problem several words downstream.

whyCorrect: The subject of the blank is 'behavioral economists such as Gino,' which is plural; 'whose research focuses on worker productivity' is a nonessential clause sitting between the subject and its verb. A plural subject in the present takes the plural verb 'contend.'

whyWrong.B: 'Is contending' is singular and agrees with Gino rather than with 'economists.'
whyWrong.C: 'Has contended' is singular; the plural present perfect would be 'have contended.'
whyWrong.D: 'Contends' is the singular present form, pulled in by the nearby name Gino instead of the actual plural subject.

commonMistakes: Matching the verb to the last noun before it instead of to the head of the subject phrase.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence about what geophysicists rely on, and everything after is another complete sentence: 'the US Geological Survey compiles such data in several ways.' The phrase 'For the Imperial fault in Imperial County, California,' is an introductory modifier belonging to that second sentence. A period is the only option that separates the two independent clauses.

whyWrong.A: 'Features for the Imperial fault...' attaches the phrase to the first clause and leaves the second clause spliced on after a comma.
whyWrong.B: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: 'And' with no comma before it still fuses two independent clauses, and the second clause remains improperly attached.

whyCorrect: Before the blank you have a complete sentence ending in 'an important list.' What follows, 'the Hawaii Register of Historic Places,' is just a noun phrase naming that list. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that introduces a specification of this kind.

whyWrong.B: A period leaves 'The Hawaii Register of Historic Places' standing alone with no verb, a fragment.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and the material after the blank is only a noun phrase.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation, 'an important list the Hawaii Register of Historic Places' runs two nouns together with nothing linking them.

tips: Colon or semicolon comes down to what follows: a semicolon needs a full sentence after it, a colon accepts a phrase.

whyCorrect: The subject of the blank is 'her book's musings on tenth-century Japanese courtly life,' and the head noun is the plural 'musings.' The singular nouns 'life' and 'Shonagon' sitting nearby do not control the verb. A plural subject in the present takes 'fascinate.'

whyWrong.A: 'Has fascinated' is singular; the plural would be 'have fascinated.'
whyWrong.B: 'Fascinates' is the singular present form and agrees with 'life' rather than with 'musings.'
whyWrong.D: 'Is fascinating' is singular and would need to be 'are fascinating.'

commonMistakes: Letting the long prepositional phrase after the subject decide the verb.

whyCorrect: The verb 'select' takes 'which sites to add next' as its direct object, and nothing separates a verb from its own object. The blank therefore takes no punctuation at all.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and 'which sites to add next to the growing registry' is not one.
whyWrong.B: A colon must follow a complete clause; 'gathers to select' is incomplete without its object.
whyWrong.C: A comma here cuts the verb off from the object it requires.

tips: If removing the punctuation leaves a smooth verb-plus-object phrase, no punctuation is the answer.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences describe one moon, Elara, and its prograde orbit. The blank sentence moves to a different moon, Pasiphae, and reports the opposite kind of orbit. What changes is the location you would visit, so the transition needs to shift the setting, and 'Elsewhere' does that.

whyWrong.A: 'For example' would make Pasiphae an instance of what was just described, but its retrograde orbit is the opposite of Elara's prograde one.
whyWrong.B: 'Specifically' narrows down the previous statement, yet this sentence introduces a new moon and a contrasting case.
whyWrong.C: 'In other words' means a restatement of the same idea; a reversed orbital direction is not a restatement.

commonMistakes: This item's stem reads 'conforms to the conventions of Standard English,' but the choices are transitions — answer it as a transition question.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the reason: voters were impressed by the album and its contribution to norteño. The second gives what they did about it: they gave the group Best Norteno Album. The transition has to mark the award as the consequence of the favorable impression, and 'Accordingly' does that.

whyWrong.A: 'In contrast' sets up an opposition, but giving an award follows naturally from being impressed.
whyWrong.C: 'Meanwhile' marks something happening at the same time but unrelated; the award is directly caused by the impression.
whyWrong.D: 'Nevertheless' would mean they gave the award despite being impressed, which is incoherent.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank describes the project loosely: turbines located off the Virginia coast. The blank sentence replaces that with exact figures, 176 turbines at a site 27 miles east of Virginia Beach. The transition must signal a move from the general to the precise.

whyWrong.A: 'In conclusion' signals a final summing-up, but this sentence adds new specifics rather than closing the discussion.
whyWrong.B: 'In contrast' requires an opposition, and the exact numbers agree with the general description.
whyWrong.C: 'As a result' would make the turbine count a consequence of the turbines being offshore, which is not a causal relationship.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize distance, so the sentence has to carry the mileage. Only one choice pairs the route from Montana to Missouri with the figure of 1,900 miles. The others use accurate notes but report dates, motives, or the modern reenactment instead.

whyWrong.A: This gives the anniversary year, which is a date, not a distance.
whyWrong.C: This states the purpose of the ride and includes no measure of how far they went.
whyWrong.D: This is about Cedeno's 2022 reenactment and says nothing about the length of the journey.

whyCorrect: The goal is to give a specific example of an onomatopoeia, which means the sentence has to quote an actual word and say what sound it imitates. Only one choice does: 'doki doki,' the Japanese word for the sound of a heartbeat.

whyWrong.A: This states the general cause of cross-language variation and quotes no word at all.
whyWrong.C: This says the two languages use different words for a heartbeat but never supplies either word, so no example is given.
whyWrong.D: This defines the term and gives its Greek roots, which is etymology rather than an example of an onomatopoeia in use.

commonMistakes: Treating a sentence that talks about examples as if it provided one.

whyCorrect: 'Recount the sequence' means the sentence has to lay the events out in order: Chrysalis approaches Saturn, tidal forces tear it apart, and the debris becomes the rings. Only one choice runs that full chain, with the 160-million-year timeframe attached.

whyWrong.A: This reverses cause and effect, making ring debris break up the moon, and its date is garbled.
whyWrong.B: This gives only the starting point and the breakup, leaving out the close approach, the tidal forces, and the rings, so there is no sequence.
whyWrong.D: This states the general physical principle about moons and tidal forces without narrating anything that happened to Chrysalis.

whyCorrect: The word 'conversely' tells you the blank is the opposite of 'historically significant.' A reign that is not significant is one that had little effect. 'Inconsequential' means exactly that: producing no important results.

whyWrong.A: 'Benevolent' means kindly, which describes a ruler's character rather than the importance of a reign.
whyWrong.B: 'Momentous' is a synonym for historically significant, so it destroys the contrast 'conversely' sets up.
whyWrong.D: 'Genuine' means authentic, which does not oppose 'significant' and would oddly imply a reign could be fake.

whyCorrect: The second sentence tells you what the fellowship does: it was given to Mary Holiday Black 'to celebrate her lifetime contributions.' The blank names that action in the first sentence, so it must mean to publicly honor or acknowledge. 'Recognize' is the standard word for it.

whyWrong.A: 'Startle' means to surprise or alarm, which is not what an award does for the artists it honors.
whyWrong.C: 'Familiarize' needs an object being made familiar with something, and the sentence has the artists as the direct object of the verb.
whyWrong.D: 'Convey' means to communicate or transport something, and you do not convey an artist.

whyCorrect: The colon means the blank restates 'juxtaposition,' and the phrase after it makes the sense concrete: sleek contemporary elements and traditional organic materials brought together 'in a single design.' The blank must therefore name the act of combining two things into one. 'Synthesis' is that word.

whyWrong.A: 'Designation' means naming or assigning, which says nothing about combining materials.
whyWrong.B: 'Analysis' means breaking something into parts, the opposite of joining elements in one design.
whyWrong.C: 'Diffusion' means spreading out or dispersing, not merging.

tips: A colon signals that the phrase after it defines the phrase before it — use the second half to fix the meaning of the blank.

whyCorrect: The colon explains the blank: what drives clustering in one industry 'may not be especially relevant among other industries.' So the causes differ from case to case. 'Variable' means changing from one instance to another, which is precisely that.

whyWrong.A: 'Unknown' would mean economists cannot identify the causes, but the sentence says the causes exist and differ by industry, not that they are undiscovered.
whyWrong.B: 'Impressive' is an evaluation and does not describe how the causes differ across industries.
whyWrong.C: 'Focused' would suggest the causes are narrow or concentrated, the opposite of varying by industry.

whyCorrect: 'Although' sets up a contrast with the second half, where recent fossil analyses have 'sharpened our picture.' Something can only be sharpened if it was blurry to begin with, so the blank must mean vague or unclear. 'Nebulous' means hazy and ill-defined.

whyWrong.A: 'Intricate' means complex in detail, which is not the opposite of a sharpened picture; detailed knowledge would not need sharpening.
whyWrong.B: 'Unprecedented' means never seen before, which describes novelty rather than vagueness.
whyWrong.C: 'Concrete' means definite and clear, so it points the same direction as 'sharpened' and kills the contrast.

whyCorrect: The first sentence reports what Devine's study concluded about ocean acidification and fish behavior. Everything after 'However' is about a weakness in that result: the sample averaged only about 25 fish, and Clark's review warns that such small samples invite biased analysis and exaggerated effects. So the text gives a finding and then raises a worry about it.

whyWrong.B: The text is about study methodology, not about describing any trait of the fish species itself.
whyWrong.C: The two studies are not compared for similarity; the second review is used to question the first study's sample size.
whyWrong.D: No solution is offered anywhere; the passage ends on the risk of exaggerated effects.

whyCorrect: Sentence one describes the Hibulb Cultural Center and how it uses traditional knowledge for its exhibits. Sentence two says the Turtle Mountain Band's center does something similar. Sentence three turns to museums that are not Indigenous-led and notes how their audiences and design strategies differ. Two tribal centers, then a comparison with non-Indigenous institutions.

whyWrong.A: The text never says the two kinds of institutions display the same artifacts, and it does not analyze any specific exhibit.
whyWrong.B: No audience reactions are reported for either kind of institution; the text is about who exhibits are designed for, not how visitors respond.
whyWrong.D: Nothing marks one center's approach as earlier and the other's as newer — the second is explicitly called 'similar.'

whyCorrect: The text lays out a chain: petroleum extraction is carbon-intensive, social attitudes increasingly favor lower-carbon energy, and therefore demand for petroleum falls. The claim about demand is that shifting societal preference drives it down, which makes drilling equipment a liability rather than an asset.

whyWrong.A: The text says the opposite — falling demand and lower prices directly threaten extraction companies' ability to recover maintenance costs.
whyWrong.C: No cycle, annual or otherwise, is described; the change is a one-directional shift in attitudes.
whyWrong.D: Declining demand is presented as a harm to these companies, turning assets into liabilities, not a benefit.

commonMistakes: This item is mis-split in the database: part of the passage appears inside the stem, so read everything before 'What claim' as the text.

whyCorrect: Alfonzo's point is that our understanding of walking decisions is not robust because different studies each spotlight one factor - demographics in some, transit availability in others - while real decisions are made in complex contexts where multiple conditions interact. If no single condition is doing the work, then no study should expect one factor to predict walking reliably.

whyWrong.A: Copying a single feature of a walkable city is exactly what the first sentence says may be insufficient, so cataloguing shared features is not the fix she proposes.
whyWrong.C: She stresses the complexity of the contexts in which choices are made; she never accuses studies of exaggerating differences between people.
whyWrong.D: She does not identify any single most important factor that studies overlook — her claim is that no one factor dominates.

whyCorrect: The word 'putatively' is the hinge: the author flags the famous reading of the invisible hand as merely supposed. Kennedy's evidence is that Smith used the metaphor once, on a narrow point about mercantilism, and that it was ignored until twentieth-century economists promoted it to give their own views a distinguished ancestry. The main idea is therefore that the metaphor's fame comes from that later promotion, not from its role in Smith's own work.

whyWrong.B: The text says the single use made a narrow point about mercantilism, not that the metaphor was a subtle critique of it, and the passage's focus is on how the metaphor got famous.
whyWrong.C: The author never endorses the metaphor as a useful model; the whole point is that its status was manufactured later.
whyWrong.D: This has the later economists discovering genuine merit, whereas the text says they elevated it because it suited views they already held.

whyCorrect: The claim requires one quotation that shows both sides of the speaker's ambivalence: dislike and acknowledged value. Only one line carries both, pairing 'a perfect contempt for it' with the discovery that 'there is in it after all, a place for the genuine.'

whyWrong.A: This affirms that business documents and school-books are important, offering no displeasure at all.
whyWrong.B: This criticizes what 'half poets' produce, so it shows only the negative half of the ambivalence.
whyWrong.C: This complains that derivative poems become unintelligible, again only dissatisfaction with no acknowledgment of merit.

commonMistakes: This item is a verbatim duplicate of another 'Poetry' question in Test 27 Module 1.

whyCorrect: The conclusion names both bacteria: D. fermentans and A. marincola might each have contributed to the rise of multicellularity. The behavior that matters is colony formation, since colonies are the multicellular step Alegado is studying. So the supporting finding has to show S. rosetta forming colonies after exposure to both species, not just one.

whyWrong.A: This supports A. marincola only and actively undercuts the half of the conclusion about D. fermentans.
whyWrong.B: Testing whether exposure amount affects colony rate is a methodological detail; it does not show either bacterium induces colonies at all.
whyWrong.C: This is the mirror image of A, supporting D. fermentans while contradicting the claim about A. marincola.

tips: When a conclusion names two items, a finding that supports only one of them weakens the other half.

whyCorrect: The claim is specifically about why Newland is late: he enjoys anticipating a pleasure. The quotation has to state that preference directly, and one does - thinking over a pleasure to come gave him 'a subtler satisfaction than its realisation.' That is the taste for anticipation the narrator uses to explain his lateness.

whyWrong.A: This is about the social respectability of arriving in a hired carriage, not about anticipation.
whyWrong.C: This establishes that he was late and had no reason to be, which is the fact needing explanation rather than the explanation itself.
whyWrong.D: This praises the opera's staging and says nothing about Newland's attitude toward pleasures still to come.

whyCorrect: The puzzle the blank must resolve is why conservationists were content even though almost all the proposed measures targeted birds. The only way that follows is if the bird-focused measures happen to protect arthropods too, since anything that reduces highway noise in the area reduces it for every animal there.

whyWrong.B: Variation among bird species says nothing about whether arthropods are covered, which is the gap the conservationists were satisfied about.
whyWrong.C: How well-documented each group's noise effects are does not make the proposed measures sufficient.
whyWrong.D: Bird measures harming arthropods would give conservationists a reason to object, the opposite of being satisfied.

tips: With 'because ______' after a 'despite' clause, the blank must explain away the shortfall just named.

whyCorrect: The text identifies the source of the MCS's high cost: longitudinal work requires years of data collection. The blank has to explain why the fitness study escapes that cost, so it must say the fitness study does not need that long time frame. Counting what share of a city's regular exercisers lift weights can be answered from a single round of data.

whyWrong.A: Whether 19,000 participants is enough for the MCS says nothing about the fitness study's budget.
whyWrong.B: If longitudinal methods were suitable for the fitness study, it would need years of collection too and would be expensive, which contradicts the sentence.
whyWrong.D: Adding questions to the MCS is about the expensive study, not about why the cheap one is cheap.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has its main verb: the chapter 'was the subject of a profile.' What follows the blank describes the profile, so it needs a modifying form, not a second conjugated verb. The participle 'appearing' attaches cleanly to 'profile' and gives 'a profile appearing in the Navajo Times on August 22, 2013.'

whyWrong.B: 'Has appeared' is a finite verb, so the sentence would have two main verbs with no conjunction joining them.
whyWrong.C: 'Appeared' is likewise finite and creates the same run-on problem after 'was.'
whyWrong.D: 'Appears' is finite and also clashes in tense with the 2013 date and with 'was.'

tips: If the sentence already has a subject and a verb, the blank almost always needs a modifier rather than another verb.

whyCorrect: Read the whole span: 'Some of these appear as lists in "Splendid Things."' is a complete sentence, and the next sentence starts with 'Shonagon catalogs.' 'In "Splendid Things"' is an ordinary prepositional phrase telling you where the lists appear, and nothing separates a noun from the prepositional phrase modifying it. No punctuation belongs in the blank.

whyWrong.B: The comma cuts 'lists' off from the phrase that identifies where they appear, an unnecessary break.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete clause, and 'appear as lists in' ends on a dangling preposition.
whyWrong.D: A colon after 'lists' leaves the fragment 'in "Splendid Things"' standing alone before the period.

commonMistakes: As transcribed, the passage puts a period inside the closing quotation mark after 'Splendid Things,' which makes the following words a separate sentence; the item appears to have lost a comma there, so read the punctuation exactly as printed.

whyCorrect: There is already a dash before 'a durable and flexible,' opening a description of black ash. That interruption has to be closed with a matching dash so the main sentence can resume: Kelly Church uses black ash to craft baskets. Only 'material—to' supplies the partner dash.

whyWrong.A: A colon cannot close an interruption opened by a dash, and it wrongly promises an explanation.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides; 'to craft baskets that are both beautiful and whimsical' is an infinitive phrase.
whyWrong.D: A period leaves the opening dash unclosed and turns 'To craft baskets that are both beautiful and whimsical' into a fragment.

tips: One dash in a sentence usually means the answer supplies the second.

whyCorrect: The material between the commas modifies Pascal, and the main verb of the sentence is 'is not an object-oriented language.' Pascal is the thing being used by other people, so the modifier needs the past participle: 'Pascal, used in software development and educational instruction, is not...'

whyWrong.A: 'To use' is an infinitive and cannot serve as a descriptive phrase attached to Pascal.
whyWrong.C: 'The use' is a noun phrase and leaves the interrupter without any verb form connecting it to Pascal.
whyWrong.D: 'Using' makes Pascal the one doing the using, but a language does not use software development; it is used in it.

whyCorrect: Cross out the nonessential clause 'whose boundaries encompass 83,400 acres' and the sentence is 'The chapter ______ known as Doo Alk'ai.' The subject is one chapter, and the fact is presented in the present, so the verb is 'is.'

whyWrong.A: 'Are' is plural and agrees with 'boundaries' inside the interrupting clause rather than with 'chapter.'
whyWrong.B: 'Have been' is plural; the singular would be 'has been.'
whyWrong.C: 'Were' is plural and also shifts to the past for a fact that is still true.

whyCorrect: The subject is 'lost works like Euripides's play about the hero Alcmaeon,' with the plural noun 'works' as its head. Everything after it, including the title and the dashed remark 'no copy of which exists,' is modification. A plural subject takes the plural verb 'have become.'

whyWrong.B: 'Becomes' is singular and agrees with the nearest noun rather than with 'works.'
whyWrong.C: 'Has become' is likewise singular.
whyWrong.D: 'Is becoming' is singular and its progressive aspect wrongly suggests the change is still under way.

commonMistakes: Letting the singular title that sits right before the blank pull the verb into the singular.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the fabric was flexible enough for Elvis to dance in. The second says the embroidered feathers added weight that probably restricted his movement. Those pull in opposite directions on the same question of mobility, so the transition must signal a contrast.

whyWrong.B: 'Firstly' opens a list, but this is the second sentence and no enumeration is under way.
whyWrong.C: 'In other words' claims the second sentence restates the first, yet it reverses the point about mobility.
whyWrong.D: 'For this reason' would make the restricted movement a consequence of the fabric's flexibility, which is backwards.

whyCorrect: The blank sentence admits something that cuts against the opening claim that Modernista architects championed nature: Torre Cortes's wavy wall and botanical window dressings could not actually grow in a forest. The next sentence then begins with 'Still' and restores the original point. That concession-then-rebuttal shape calls for 'Granted.'

whyWrong.B: 'Similarly' claims agreement with the preceding sentence, but this one raises a limitation on it.
whyWrong.C: 'Furthermore' adds more support for the claim, whereas this sentence pushes against it — which is why 'Still' is needed afterward.
whyWrong.D: 'Thus' presents a conclusion drawn from the first sentence; saying the building could not grow in a forest does not follow from architects championing nature.

tips: A 'Still' or 'Nevertheless' in the following sentence is a strong sign the blank is a concession.

whyCorrect: The second half of the sentence names the consequence of the first half: by serving in the 18th New York Cavalry, Johnson became one of the few Chinese-born American soldiers of the war. The transition must tie the outcome to the act that produced it, and 'in doing so' does that.

whyWrong.A: 'Usually' marks something habitual, but this is a single historical outcome, not a pattern.
whyWrong.B: 'For instance' would make his place in history an example of his service, when it is the result of that service.
whyWrong.C: 'In any case' dismisses what came before as not mattering, yet his service is exactly what earned him the place.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize a difference between the two supercontinents, so the sentence must set their formation dates against each other. Only one choice does: Euramerica formed far later than Ur, which formed about 3.1 billion years ago.

whyWrong.B: This describes the supercontinent cycle in general and names neither Ur nor Euramerica, so nothing is contrasted.
whyWrong.C: This states what the two have in common, which is the opposite of the stated goal.
whyWrong.D: This gives only Ur's date and fate; with no second item there is no difference to see.

commonMistakes: The date for Euramerica is garbled in this choice ('about million years ago'), but it is still the only option that contrasts the two.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain what national union federations are for. The notes say the SSWTUF, a national federation, helps improve conditions for workers in its nation. The sentence therefore has to state that purpose and use the SSWTUF as the illustration, which only one choice does.

whyWrong.A: This describes the relationship between the SSWTUF and a regional federation, not the purpose of national federations.
whyWrong.B: This explains what regional federations do, which is the wrong level of organization.
whyWrong.D: This identifies the SSWTUF's type and location but says nothing about what such federations exist to do.

whyCorrect: To contrast the two refuges, the sentence has to name both and put a difference between them. Only one does, setting the James River NWR in Virginia on the Atlantic against Hopper Mountain in California on the Pacific.

whyWrong.B: This mentions only the James River NWR, so there is nothing to contrast it with.
whyWrong.C: This states what the two refuges have in common, the opposite of a contrast.
whyWrong.D: This is a general statement about NWRs and endangered species and names only one of the two refuges.

whyCorrect: The example tells you what the method accomplishes: because Malmendier is cited very often, we can tell her work 'has been quite significant.' Counting citations is a way of gauging importance, so the blank needs a verb meaning to measure or judge. 'Assess' is that verb.

whyWrong.B: 'Utilize' means to put to use, but tracking citations does not make use of a scholar's importance.
whyWrong.C: 'Influence' would mean citation counts change how important the research is, rather than reveal it.
whyWrong.D: 'Undermine' means to weaken, which contradicts an example showing frequent citation as evidence of significance.

whyCorrect: The 'but' splits the sentence into a helpful design feature and a harmful one. Since the second half describes a robot unsettling people, the first half must describe something that increases their ease. 'Buttress' means to strengthen or support, so voice-command response bolsters people's comfort.

whyWrong.A: 'Constrict' means to squeeze or limit, which would reduce comfort and destroy the contrast with the uncanny valley.
whyWrong.B: 'Repudiate' means to reject a claim, and feelings of comfort are not something a robot feature rejects.
whyWrong.D: 'Mitigate' means to lessen, so it points the same direction as the negative half of the sentence instead of opposing it.

tips: 'But' tells you the two halves must go in opposite directions — fix the direction before picking the word.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with 'To improve this system,' and the example given is the postage stamp, which shifts payment to the sender and closes off the recipients' dodges. The blank names the things proposed for that purpose: changes intended to correct a flawed system. 'Reforms' is exactly that.

whyWrong.A: 'Investigations' are inquiries into a problem, but a postage stamp is a fix, not an inquiry.
whyWrong.B: 'Expansions' would mean making the existing system bigger, whereas the stamp changes how it works.
whyWrong.D: 'Possessions' means owned objects and cannot be 'proposed' to improve a system.

whyCorrect: The passage says the air-sac structures themselves do not usually fossilize, so researchers cannot observe them directly. Instead they look for indirect clues, such as large holes in the bones. Drawing a conclusion from indirect evidence is inferring, so the blank must be 'infer.'

whyWrong.B: 'Acquire' would mean physically obtaining the structures, which is impossible since they do not fossilize.
whyWrong.C: 'Isolated' is the wrong form for the infinitive slot after 'To,' and isolating a structure again implies it is physically there.
whyWrong.D: 'Preserve' means keeping something from decaying, but the researchers are studying fossils long after any preservation could occur.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank says elements of the mission style 'have been reproduced throughout the state,' and Santa Clara University is offered as the example. The blank therefore has to mean copying that style. 'Imitate' is the direct match for 'reproduced.'

whyWrong.A: 'Renovate' means to repair or update an existing structure, but Santa Clara University is a separate building modeled on the missions, not a restoration of them.
whyWrong.C: 'Neglect' means to ignore, which contradicts the statement that the style has been reproduced.
whyWrong.D: 'Reject' would mean the design refuses the mission style, the opposite of being an example of its spread.

whyCorrect: The text names one feature of the Aubrey/Maturin books, their abrupt endings, and then reports two readings of it. Some critics call the endings arbitrary failures to conclude; others say the books should be read as one continuous work, in which case abrupt breaks are not flaws at all. The passage supplies both views without settling between them.

whyWrong.A: The author never claims The Hundred Days is among O'Brian's most complex books or offers a reason for such a ranking.
whyWrong.B: Proust is mentioned only as a comparison for multivolume form; no argument about literary renown is made.
whyWrong.D: Entertainment value is never discussed, and the second group of critics denies that the structure is a flaw rather than excusing it.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences cover Parton's late 1970s and early 1980s country-pop records and her commercial peak. Then 'A decade earlier, however' moves back in time to her roots as a songwriter in Blue Ridge folk tradition, with 'Jolene' as the example. The structure is one period of her career followed by an earlier one.

whyWrong.A: No debate about pop influence on 'Jolene' appears; the song is cited as evidence of folk-ballad influence.
whyWrong.C: The text neither recommends the early work nor expresses disappointment with the later work, which it credits with her greatest success.
whyWrong.D: The text does not claim the two songs resemble each other; it uses them to mark two different phases.

whyCorrect: The detail is in the sentence naming the cofounders: Hooks and Ward 'had met while performing in a 1960 touring production of Lorraine Hansberry's play A Raisin in the Sun.' Both were performers in that production, which is how they first met.

whyWrong.A: Harrison is the playwright whose work NEC produced in 1974; the text never has him introducing anyone.
whyWrong.B: The Great MacDaddy was produced in 1974, seven years after they founded NEC together, so it cannot be where they met.
whyWrong.C: NEC's workshops came after the company existed, and the meeting predates the company by seven years.

whyCorrect: The author's complaint about the energy ladder is that it is 'reductive,' not that it is false. The concession 'although income of course constrained fuel choice' keeps income as a genuine factor, while Hosier and Dowd's Zimbabwe work adds others, such as how hard fuel is to obtain. So income accounts for part of the variation in fuel choice but not all of it.

whyWrong.B: The author explicitly grants that income constrains fuel choice, so denying any effect goes further than the text.
whyWrong.C: The objection is that the model leaves factors out, not that it misidentifies why income matters.
whyWrong.D: The whole discussion is about which type of fuel households choose; no distinction between amount and type is drawn.

tips: 'Reductive' is a charge of incompleteness, not of error — that distinction separates the right answer from the overstatement.

whyCorrect: The claim about wireless devices is narrow: a steady energy load is 'an absolute prerequisite' for powering them piezoelectrically. To support that, you need evidence that unsteady power actually breaks such devices. Showing that intermittent or unpredictable supply undermines their efficacy is exactly that evidence.

whyWrong.A: If ordinary non-CFRP harvesters could already power these devices, the new steady-output design would not be a prerequisite for anything.
whyWrong.C: Incompatibility with most wireless devices would undercut the passage's point rather than support it.
whyWrong.D: This is about the amount of energy the electrode makes possible, while the claim at issue is about steadiness of supply.

commonMistakes: Supporting the sentence's overall subject rather than the one clause the question names.

whyCorrect: The claim has two requirements: an irrigation practice used in the Southwest today, and an origin well before 1890. The Hohokam quotation supplies both, describing 7th-century hydraulic engineering principles in what is now central Arizona that today's engineers still use.

whyWrong.B: This says irrigation matters greatly today but gives no historical depth at all.
whyWrong.C: This dates the expansion to after the Second World War, which is later than 1890, not earlier.
whyWrong.D: Sprinkler systems were developed in the late 20th century, so they postdate Searsville Lake rather than predating it.

whyCorrect: The claim is specifically that the house has faded over time, so the quotation must show both the original appearance and its loss. One does: the house had once been painted, the sun blistered the paint and the rain washed it away, and it is now 'as dull and gray as everything else.'

whyWrong.A: This describes fences and a farmhouse painted green, which is fresh color rather than fading, and a different house.
whyWrong.B: This is about Dorothy getting a drink and preparing for her journey, with no description of the house's condition.
whyWrong.D: This describes the gray prairie stretching in every direction, the surroundings rather than the house's changed appearance.

tips: For 'illustrates the claim,' check that the quotation contains the change the claim describes, not just the end state.
